source.title: CodeChameleon: Personalized Encryption Framework for Jailbreaking Large Language Models
source.authors: Huijie Lv; Xiao Wang; Yuansen Zhang; Cai-Shuang Huang; Shi-Han Dou; Junjie Ye; Tao Gui; Qi Zhang; Xuan-Jing Huang

record.tranche_reason: Tests whether a compliant positive response opening bypasses safety using a prefilled-start intervention and harmful-response rates, a different method from the fine-tuning and token-position measurements in the claim.
record.gate_note: The paper also reports personalized-encryption and code-format jailbreak attack success rates. These test a bypass mechanism not named in the claim versions, so they are recorded under fits_no_version. Table 3 measures decryption validity, not safety behavior. Figure 3 reports ASR changes for encryption and decryption ablations; the text gives some changes but does not clearly map all reported values to individual models or conditions.
record.test_reason: Section 4.3/Table 4 prefills a positive response beginning on Llama2-Chat 7B/13B/70B with unencrypted harmful queries. It reports harmful-content ASR of 88–99%, which bears directly on V4's prefilling bypass. The main CodeChameleon results are an encryption jailbreak, not a version of the claim.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors hypothesize that safety works as intent recognition followed by response generation, and that CodeChameleon's encryption plus code format evades the recognition step (77.5% average ASR). They read the prefill result (Table 4: harmful output in over 90% of cases) as showing that once recognition is bypassed, models tend to comply.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses adversarial prompts with personalized query encryption, embedded decryption instructions, and a code-completion template. It does not fine-tune models or measure token-position KL divergence.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported outcomes vary across the four encryption functions, code-style versus text-style instructions, and whether encryption/decryption components are included. Positive-opening ASRs also vary across model sizes and table columns.

fits_no_version.finding: CodeChameleon encryption plus code-completion prompts reach 65.4–86.6% ASR across seven models, averaging 77.5%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Personalized encryption combined with code-completion instructions jailbreaks aligned chat models.

fits_no_version.finding: On Llama2-Chat, ASR varies by encryption function: 46.2–86.5%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Encryption-jailbreak success depends on the encryption function and on model size.

record.problems: The paper notes that the evaluated model variety is insufficient and that its analysis and ablations focus on open-source Llama2. The positive-opening table reports post-intervention ASRs but no corresponding unprefixed baseline rates. GPT-4 is used as the ASR evaluator; human evaluation checks 100 GPT-4-1106 outputs and reports 93% agreement.

untested.parts: Adversarial suffixes and decoding changes. The prefill is not varied by number of tokens, and there is no token-position analysis.
All of it: no harmful fine-tuning.
All of it: no benign fine-tuning.
All of it: no per-token KL measurements.
All of it: no parameter localization.
All of it: the study proposes an intent-recognition hypothesis but does not test a data or objective cause.
All of it: no deepening training.

missing.what: ASR without encryption or decryption (direct malicious queries, no prefill) on Llama2-Chat. This is the natural no-prefill baseline for Table 4. The text only says it is low ('challenging').

record.verdict_notes: The prefill experiment uses a sub-dataset of unstated size. The Table 4 columns (Reverse/Length/OddEven/BinaryTree) correspond to template variants even though the queries are unencrypted. The GPT-4 judge was checked against humans on GPT-4 outputs only (93% agreement). Rows r13–r31 measure the study's own attack and are correctly unlinked.

versions.untested_parts: Fine-tuning on harmful examples and its effect on refusal.
Fine-tuning on ordinary or carefully selected benign data.
Per-token KL divergence between aligned and base models across response positions.
Suffixes and decoding changes; the paper tests a manually prefixed positive response opening.
Whether safety is localized in a small set of weights or ranks.
Whether training data or objectives produce safety shallowness.
Training that spreads safety beyond the first tokens and whether it remains effective.

rows.subject: Llama2-Chat 7B
rows.operation_detail: Manually prefixed the response with a positive reply beginning; malicious queries were not encrypted.
rows.measure: Attack Success Rate (ASR), harmful content generation
rows.note: The table reports the ASR for a positive-response beginning. The text says the model continues from the supplied beginning.
rows.check: Should be linked to V4. There is no numeric unprefilled baseline; the text says direct malicious queries rarely succeed (Figure 3, w/o en_de). The prefill sits inside the code-style template with refusal-suppression rules, and the column label names the decryption function shown, not encryption.

relationships.condition: Llama2-Chat 7B/13B/70B, positive reply prefilled in SFT format, unencrypted harmful queries in the code-style template, GPT-4 judge
relationships.reason: Prefilled ASR is 88–99% across all sizes and templates (r1–r12), against direct queries the text says rarely succeed. The template also includes refusal suppression, which confounds the prefill effect.
relationships.display_finding: Attack success was 88–99% across all sizes and templates, while direct queries rarely succeeded, though the template's refusal suppression confounds the prefill effect.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.reason: The reported harmful-content ASRs are 88%–99% across the table conditions, consistent with positive-prefill bypassing refusal (r1–r12).
